newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba seeks to avoid incident around Spanish embassy.
newsitem.headline: Cuba seeks to avoid incident around Spanish embassy.

text.p: Cuba, engaged in a diplomatic spat with Spain but seeking to prevent any incident around the Spanish Embassy, Wednesday denied rumours among Cubans that Spain has changed its visa policy for Cubans.
Cuban authorities also posted a heavy security cordon around the Spanish Embassy building, closing off streets to traffic in the immediate area, to prevent any disturbances.
The Foreign Ministry issued a statement saying that in response to a request from the Spanish Embassy it was informing the public that the Spanish consular service was operating normally.
Opening hours and procedures for visa requests and other embassy business remained the same, the statement said.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs adds that rumours that the granting of visas by this (Spanish) consulate in a more rapid or special way are totally false," the statement added.

Crowds of several hundred people gathered around the embassy building Tuesday following news Cuba had protested strongly to the Spanish government over what it viewed as meddling in its internal affairs. Cuba said it was withdrawing its official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.

The crowds appeared to be partly people curious to see if anything was happening, and partly Cubans thinking that there might be an increased chance of obtaining a visa or seeking asylum in the embassy.
There was a moment of tension Tuesday evening when several dozen people tried to break through the security cordon around the embassy. Reporters saw several people detained.

By Wednesday morning hundreds of police and members of civilian order groups stood guard on the streets around the embassy, which were closed to traffic. Their presence deterred fresh crowds from forming in the area.

A planned government-organised student march, unrelated to the diplomatic crisis, was due to pass near the embassy area Wednesday afternoon. The march through Havana is held annually each November 27 to mark the anniversary of the death by firing squad of eight medical students under Spanish colonial rule in the 19th century.
Relations between Spain and Cuba, which have strong historical, cultural and economic ties, are at their lowest point since 1990, when there was a crisis over asylum-seekers.

Tuesday's move by Cuba followed steady criticism of President Fidel Castro's communist government by the conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, which has adopted a tougher line on Havana than its Socialist predecessor.
